newsitem.title: USA: US Budget, taxes top Republican list - Senate's Lott.
newsitem.headline: US Budget, taxes top Republican list - Senate's Lott.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Wednesday the Republican legislative priorities for the coming year include a balanced budget, a multi-year tax cut package worth $100-$150 billion, and several plans sought by business to ease government regulations.

Outlining his party's ideas for the new congressional session in a speech before the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Lott said President Clinton's cabinet will be given early approval with one or two exceptions. U.S. Trade Representative nominee Charlene Barshevsky is regarded with favor, but her past ties to a foreign government present legal problems, he said.

Clinton, who is to present his fiscal 1998 budget in early February, must not rely on "games" to reach a balanced budget, Lott warned. Republicans would not accept a budget that proposes higher spending now and cuts in future years, or proposes a larger deficit this year with assurances it will be lowered later.
"I believe we're going to come up with a balanced budget plan this year, that will get us to a balance budget over a period of years, by the year 2002, I presume," Lott said.

Apart from the annual budget battles, the first item on the Republican list will be a constitutional amendment to balance the budget. However, Lott said the timing of the vote has not been set. The Senate failed to pass it by one vote last year after it passed the House, but its chances are thought to have improved with the election in November of more supporters.

Lott said he had indications from the White House that Clinton would consider capital gains tax relief that included more than his proposed real estate gains tax cut. Lott would also like the capital gains tax to be indexed to inflation, a change that would give taxpayers additional protection against gains resulting from inflation.

The tax cut, which would be through fiscal 2002, would be considered in context of the fiscal 1998 budget, he said. The size of the tax cut would depend on how much money is available in keeping with the budget goals, he said.

In addition, the Republicans would like changes in estate taxes to reduce the amount of taxes paid upon transfer of assets after death. "I would like to eliminate it completely," he said. Over the next several years, Congress must look at major revisions of income taxes paid by individuals and corporations, he added.

Other items on the Republican agenda will include changes in the Superfund toxic waste clean-up laws, regulatory reform, legislation to permit compensatory time in lieu of paid overtime, highway construction legislation and campaign reform, he said.

One item Lott did not want on Congress's table would be revision of the recently passed welfare reform law. Although states have protested against some of its provisions, particularly limits on benefits to legal immigrants, it should be allowed to work for a year before changes are considered, he said.

Concerning Barshefsky's nomination, Lott said a waiver of the law on previous employment by a foreign government will be looked at, but he was reluctant to waive the law. He will meet with Barshefsky this month. "We need to think about it very carefully. I have an open mind on it but I do have some hesitancy," he said.

Two other topics, changes to the consumer price index and Social Security, will not be Republicans' immediate priorities, he added. If the CPI needs to be adjusted, it should be done after a balanced budget is reached. And, on Social Security, more study is needed through a new commission which could look at a type of personal savings accounts.
